4: This document provides evidence-based responses to the most common factually incorrect claims about Bitcoin mining and energy. It is an essential starting point for any regulator, policy-maker, journalist or curious individual who wants their beliefs about Bitcoin and energy to be anchored in fact. That means anchored in independent, up-to-date data about the Bitcoin network.
5: Every claim below was, at one time, common in mainstream media. As each was disproven, journalists stopped repeating it (not always immediately). Today these claims are largely no longer heard in mainstream media, though the odd one still surfaces from time to time. For each claim I’ve noted where it came from, why it stopped, followed by what the evidence shows. I've also included a graphic at the top documenting when each claim went out of mainstream media circulation.
8: **Why it stopped:** Peer-reviewed studies rejected the method. Then in 2023, Sai and Vranken’s review found de Vries’ body of work unreliable, which left journalists with no credible source to quote.
9: As soon as the claim came out, it was rebuked in three peer-reviewed studies ([[2|Masanet et al]]., 2019; [[3|Dittmar et al]]., 2019; [[4|Sedlmeir et al]]., 2020) as well as by [[5|Cambridge University]]. But it wasn't until [[6|Sai and Vranken]] (2023) that the media finally stopped circulating it. The claim is false for the simple reason that Bitcoin's resource use does not come from its transactions. It comes from the process of mining Bitcoin.
10: This is a critical distinction. It means that unlike the Banking system, Bitcoin's transaction volume can scale without increasing resource use (energy, water, electronics). In an age of climate consequence, a financial system that can scale without scaling its environmental impact could be very positive for humanity.
11: The original claim came from a 5-page commentary by Alex de Vries entitled "Bitcoin’s Growing Energy Problem." A commentary, unlike a paper, does not have to go through a peer review process. Commentaries are also non-empirical (they are based on theory, not the results of observation and experiments). De Vries first measured [[7|energy per transaction]]. He later extended this to the equally invalid method of measuring eWaste, emissions and water use per transaction. These studies, while flawed, made for great headlines, and so were widely cited in the media. Journalists kept quoting his commentaries until 2023, when Sai and Vranken debunked the body of de Vries' work.
12: On the specific point regarding eWaste, in 2025 Cambridge showed that de Vries’ per transaction method was not only flawed. His total eWaste estimates were also overstated by 1204% (2.3 kT eWaste, not the annual 30 kT eWaste claimed by de Vries). That invalidated de Vries’ claim that Bitcoin mining had an eWaste problem. [[8|Source]]. Cambridge's study showed that in almost all cases, and unlike consumer electronics, old Bitcoin mining rigs were reused, resold or fully recycled.
13: **Where it came from:** January 2022, when Kazakhstan’s government blamed crypto miners for a blackout across Central Asia. Its grid operator had already disconnected them before the blackout hit.
15: There is a fast-growing body of independent research which shows that Bitcoin mining in fact stabilizes grids. It is uniquely suited to this because it is flexible, modular and interruptible. This stabilizing effect has been felt most strongly on grids moving to more VRE (Variable [[9|Renewable Energy]]) such as solar and wind.
16: For example, a whitepaper from Duke University energy experts concluded that Controllable Load Resources (aka: Bitcoin mining) help to [[10|stabilize grids]] and delay expensive grid upgrades.
21: One caveat: it is possible to use Bitcoin mining in a way that destabilizes the grid (just as it is possible to misuse a hammer to commit a crime). But when these instances happen, they are both mild and rare. For example, [[15|ERCOT (Texas) grid data]] shows Bitcoin mining stabilizes the grid almost daily through two different services: [[16|Frequency Regulation]] and [[17|Demand Response]]. There have also been several large-scale emergency events where Bitcoin mining stabilized the grid. The major documented case is Texas' [[18|July 2022 heatwave]]. In contrast, [[19|ERCOT has documented]] a small number of mild, local events in which mining loads briefly dropped off the grid during transmission faults. These nudged frequency up for a few minutes without causing any outages. So over a multi-year period, large-scale grid stabilization events far outnumber these brief disturbances.
32: After the 2021 blackouts, a major solution proposed was building gas peaker plants (the Berkshire plan and later Senate Bill 6), estimated to cost [[28|$18 Billion]]. Instead, ERCOT brought in Bitcoin miners as a large, flexible load (reportedly up to 3 [[29|GW]]) that can rapidly [[30|reduce consumption during grid stress]]. Flexible demand replaced the need for more flexible generation.
34: In Sept 2024, Norwegian residents realized that Bitcoin mining had for years been keeping their power prices 20% lower. When the Bitcoin mining operation left the grid, their prices [[31|instantly increased]] to cover the revenue shortfall.
36: Then, [[32|CNBC reported]] that adding Bitcoin mining to a rural microgrid in Kenya "dropped the price of power from 35 cents per kilowatt hour to 25 cents per kWh". That was a 28.5% price cut, achieved by using hydro energy that was previously wasted.
41: The bigger reason the metric is flawed, though, is that it conflates energy use with environmental harm. The consensus in mainstream environmental science and policymaking focuses on transforming the energy system, not on reducing total energy use.
42: This is even written into the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change)’s assessment reports, which represent the broad scientific consensus. They outline a pathway that requires a major shift in __how__ energy is produced and consumed, not a blanket reduction in use. Key changes include:
44: **Where it came from:** Early academic projections made in 2018 and 2019, when there was little data on what actually powered Bitcoin mining. Those projections assumed a largely coal-powered network. That was true at the time, because Bitcoin was then using a lot of coal power from China.
46: Like electric vehicles (EVs), Bitcoin mining has no direct emissions, only scope-2 (indirect) emissions from electricity use. It also obviates a more emission-intensive technology (the banking sector; see chart below).
47: Bitcoin mining is in fact the only global industry for which there is robust, third-party data showing it has crossed the 50% [[37|sustainable energy]] threshold. The global average grid mix is about 41% low carbon, and other major sectors have no comparable industry-wide energy mix data. So it stands as a uniquely documented case of reaching this milestone at a global scale.
49: It is the generation of electricity that causes pollution, not the user of electricity. Like an EV, Bitcoin mining (sometimes called crypto mining) runs on electricity, so any pollution comes from how that electricity is generated. Over half of that electricity already comes from sustainable sources. Claiming Bitcoin mining causes pollution is as misleading as claiming EVs cause pollution. There is no universe in which it is logical to claim that Bitcoin mining causes pollution but EVs don’t, or that EVs cause pollution but Bitcoin mining doesn’t. They are precisely analogous. If we find ourselves resisting this logical equivalence, that can help uncover our implicit biases.
50: EVs accounted for 80 [[39|Mt CO2e]] of attributable [[40|GHG]] emissions in China and the US alone, but this statistic is never presented in isolation. Similarly, it is highly misleading to present Bitcoin mining’s emissions without noting they are scope-2, and without mentioning the more emission-intensive industry it replaces.
57: **Why it stopped:** Greenpeace USA’s campaign went silent in early 2024 and was [[47|reported as over in December 2024]], without a single line of Bitcoin’s code changing. By then, [[48|peer-reviewed research]] had shown that Bitcoin’s environmental benefits depend on proof of work. Proof-of-stake cryptocurrencies cannot deliver them.
60: Bitcoin’s Proof of Work algorithm means that its energy use has resulted in a proven ability to [[50|mitigate methane]] and [[51|provide stability to the energy grid]]. It can also [[52|increase renewable energy capacity]], [[53|monetize wasted renewable energy]], [[54|support renewable development and climate action]], and facilitate [[55|clean microgrid development]]. Each of these is demonstrated in the linked peer-reviewed research and independent reports.
61: Ethereum lost the capacity to deliver these environmental benefits when it moved from POW to POS in Sept 2022. For me as a climatetech investor, this was a loss. Until then, we had been looking at using both Bitcoin and Ethereum mining operations to mitigate methane from landfills. Their biogas would be turned into electricity to power crypto-mining, so the methane was not released into the air. When Ethereum changed to Proof of Stake, it was no longer useful as a potential form of climatetech.
62: Cambridge’s latest survey puts Bitcoin’s methane mitigation at [[56|4.69 MtCO2e a year]] (December 2025). That is about 11% of the network’s total emissions on [[57|BEEST 2]]’s latest figures. It reduces [[58|methane emissions]] from the O&G industry that otherwise would have gone into the atmosphere. No other form of cryptocurrency can achieve this at such a scale.
64: Methane's high global warming potential means even small-scale power generation from flared or vented gas yields major emission cuts. So nothing prevents Bitcoin mining from exceeding 100% mitigation in the future, potentially abating more emissions than it produces through methane alone. That is before counting the more emission-intensive banking sector it obviates.
65: Bitcoin mining qualifies as climatetech for its emission [[60|abatement]] capabilities. Under Proof-of-Stake, however, it couldn't deliver the benefits cited in 32 peer-reviewed papers and 8 reports. Those benefits stem from its flexible, energy-intensive Proof-of-Work mechanism.
66: The important point here is that conflating energy use with environmental harm is not only mistaken. It is something environmental scientists and a consensus of policymakers say we should avoid. Yes, when that energy use is mostly fossil fuel (as it is in the banking sector), more energy use is environmentally harmful. But when that energy use is mostly sustainable, helping to mitigate methane and accelerating renewable energy development (as Bitcoin has been shown to), more energy use promotes more climate action.
70: **Where it came from:** March 2022, after Bloomberg reported that ExxonMobil was supplying flare gas to a Bitcoin miner in North Dakota. Critics countered that the gas could go to other uses.
75: However, [[64|unique to Bitcoin mining]], ~80% of its operating costs are electricity. So there is a very strong economic incentive to find the cheapest power, even if it is remote, hard to access and needs capital spending to harness.
81: **Where it came from:** The New York Times’ 2023 investigation into Bitcoin mining, which used marginal emissions rates. These assume every new user’s demand is met by whichever power plant switches on next. On that basis, the investigation treated miners as taking clean power away from other customers.
82: **Why it stopped:** Energy researchers have since shown that short-run marginal emissions are not a credible way to measure the real impact of new electricity demand. In 2025, [[66|Bistline and Watten showed in Nature Climate Change]] that the method can overstate effects by 41–98%. Princeton’s Jesse Jenkins called it “NOT a credible measure of consequential emissions impacts.” Applied consistently, the same logic would say every electricity user takes renewable power from every other user, whether a hospital, an EV owner or a heat pump.
84: But first, let's address the claim itself. The claim is unsupported by evidence. It also contradicts the built-in economic incentive that discourages Bitcoin mining companies from ever using power when wholesale power prices spike (when other people need it).
85: Former ERCOT Grid operator [[67|Brad Jones]] described Bitcoin as a “non-rival energy user”. In other words, because it relies so heavily on cheap power, it powers down the moment the price of power becomes too expensive. That is the very time other people want or need that power.
86: What there is strong evidence for is that, as a direct result of Bitcoin mining, many people now have access to renewable energy who otherwise would not.
87: For example, Gridless in Africa has delivered renewable energy to four villages (an estimated 28,000 people). On a much bigger scale in Ethiopia, there is strong evidence from EEP data that Bitcoin mining has helped [[68|accelerate the building of transmission lines]] to deliver renewable energy to rural communities.
88: In terms of the “use for something better” argument, Bitcoin mining seeks out the cheapest energy. Much of this energy is stranded, and other users cannot use it because of its remote location, unattractive time of day, or both.
90: It is also an implicit value judgment about how we “should” use energy, often made without looking into Bitcoin’s rapidly growing list of uses. There are now [[69|21 documented environmental and humanitarian uses]] that Bitcoin currently has. Bitcoin is increasingly used to deliver important and well-documented social and environmental benefits. Without knowing this, we cannot legitimately claim that the energy used for bitcoin mining would be better used for AI, Netflix or any number of other uses.
92: **Why it stopped:** Media outlets reported more and more of Bitcoin mining’s humanitarian benefits. These ranged from microgrids bringing power to villages in Kenya and Malawi to mining heat warming homes in Finland. Once [[70|21 documented benefits]] were on the record, it became clear that “wastes” was a value judgment, not a metric.
93: This is not an accurate assessment. There is significant peer-reviewed literature and case studies showing where bitcoin mining has __prevented__ the waste of renewable energy.
94: For example, [[71|Moghimi et al]] found that traditional Microgrids produced a large amount of excess energy, which is wasted because renewable generation and demand don’t match. When Bitcoin mining was added, it prevented almost all energy waste, while cutting microgrid operating costs by 46.5%.
95: Similarly, [[72|Lai and You]] found that Bitcoin mining prevented the significant waste of power often linked to wind and solar. That waste happens when power is produced at the wrong time of day, or in the wrong location without enough transmission capacity. They found that “Leveraging crypto as virtual carriers can enhance renewable capacity and potentially achieve up to 98% and 92% utilization of available solar and wind power, respectively.”
96: Further, “wasting energy” is not an objective assessment, but a value judgment. One can only claim that energy is wasted if no good to humanity comes from it. As we've already seen in the point above, there are [[73|21 well-documented benefits]] made possible by bitcoin mining’s Proof of Work Algorithm. That is a remarkable achievement for a technology which is only 17 years old.
51: Cambridge data is very clear on this point. It attributes these emissions solely to scope-2 electricity use, not scope-1 direct impacts: “electricity usage of Bitcoin mining activity at approximately 138 [[41|TWh]], resulting in around [[42|39.8 MtCO2e attributable GHG emissions]]", a figure that is similar to Bitcoin indirect emission levels in 2019.
